  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid People: avoid other people, Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
James, a 47-year-old bus driver from a small town in North America, had always prided himself on his ability to connect with people. He remembered the warmth of the community, the familiar faces he saw daily as he navigated the same routes. But everything changed one fateful evening when he witnessed a police altercation just outside his bus. He had been preparing to pull away from the curb when he saw a young man being apprehended. The tension escalated quickly, and before James could process what was happening, he found himself frozen in place as his bus became a front-row seat to chaos. The sound of shouting, the flash of blue lights, and the palpable fear in the air felt like a scene ripped from a movie, but it was all too real. 

In the days and weeks following the incident, memories of that night invaded James’s thoughts uninvited. He had come to dread the moments when the recollection would strike him with an overwhelming intensity, often while he was trying to focus on his job. The intrusive memories would come suddenly, a visceral reminder of the panic he had felt, leaving him breathless. Just the sight of police officers in uniform would send his heart racing and his mind spiraling back to that night, as if he were still trapped in that moment. 

James’s coping strategies began to shift as he tried to manage his escalating anxiety. Initially, he would simply turn up the volume on the radio or the television at home, drowning out the chaos in his mind with loud music or noise. But as time passed, even that became insufficient. He started to avoid contact with others, retreating into his apartment whenever he could. The thought of facing people made him feel exposed and vulnerable, as if they could sense the turmoil within him. He would pull his hands over his face, a futile attempt to shield himself from the reality of his own fear and shame. 

His irritability grew, manifesting in angry outbursts that surprised even him. The simplest things would set him off—a passenger on his bus who didn’t follow the rules, a coworker who joked too loudly in the break room. He found himself snapping at people he had once considered friends, causing rifts he couldn’t quite mend. James had come to believe that the world was a perilous place, filled with unpredictability and danger. He felt a gnawing sense of isolation, a deep-rooted conviction that he had lost his connection to the community he once cherished. What frightened him most was the growing mistrust he felt towards those around him; he was convinced that people couldn’t be trusted, that they were oblivious to the chaos that lay just beneath the surface of everyday life.

As months passed, James developed a routine of checking the locks on his doors multiple times before bed, a compulsive behavior that brought him a fleeting sense of security, though it never truly eased his mind. Each click of the lock echoed the sentiment that he had to protect himself from the world outside, reinforcing his belief that danger lurked at every corner. His concentration at work suffered, and he often found himself lost in thought, staring blankly at the road ahead, wondering how he had let his life spiral into this state of disarray. 

Eventually, the weight of his symptoms became too heavy to bear alone. After a particularly explosive argument with a passenger who commented on his mood, James felt a surge of desperation that propelled him to seek help. He realized he could no longer navigate this overwhelmed state by himself. What he hoped for most was to feel safe again, to regain his connection with the world outside his apartment and the community he had once felt a part of. He feared that he would always be trapped in this cycle of anger and avoidance, but deep down, he yearned to reclaim the man he used to be, the bus driver who brought joy to others with a simple smile and a friendly wave.
